1.title: Too Big to Depeg
1.text: The 800-pound gorilla of stablecoins commands more market cap than most countries' GDP and settles more volume daily than Visa. Despite years of "where are the reserves?" discourse, Tether keeps printing — and keeps getting redeemed at par. Its BDO Italia attestations have quieted skeptics somewhat, but the real moat is simpler: when every exchange, DeFi protocol, and OTC desk denominates in USDT, switching costs approach infinity. Love it or hate it, the market has voted with its liquidity.

2.title: The Regulated Runner-Up
2.text: Circle's USDC is what happens when you build a stablecoin for compliance officers. Full monthly attestations from Deloitte, SEC registration, and a BlackRock-managed reserve fund make it the institutional darling of the space. The March 2023 SVB depeg briefly shattered its reputation for safety — and its market cap still hasn't fully recovered to pre-crisis levels. For anyone who needs a stablecoin their legal team won't flinch at, USDC remains the default.

5.title: The OG Decentralized Dollar
5.text: The stablecoin that proved crypto could create a synthetic dollar without a bank account. DAI survived the March 2020 crash, navigated the USDC depeg contagion, and maintained its peg through sheer overcollateralization. Now overshadowed by its own rebrand (USDS) and increasingly backed by RWAs rather than pure crypto collateral, DAI remains the philosophical North Star that most "decentralized" stablecoins claim to be inspired by.

6.title: The Identity Crisis
6.text: Frax started life as crypto's boldest algorithmic experiment -- a fractional-reserve stablecoin that actually worked. Then it quietly abandoned the algorithm, went 100% USDC-collateralized, and launched frxUSD backed by BlackRock's BUIDL fund. The original FRAX is now labeled "Legacy Frax Dollar" with a shrinking supply, while frxUSD chases institutional credibility. It's a remarkable pivot from "trust the math" to "trust BlackRock," and the market cap of both combined still barely registers against USDC.

7.title: The Fallen Faithful
7.text: Once positioned as the transparent alternative to Tether, TrueUSD has fallen from grace with a market cap that's a fraction of its peak. Regulatory issues, questions about its Prime Trust relationship, and a depeg incident in 2023 eroded the trust its name once implied. It persists more as a cautionary tale about counterparty risk than as a competitive stablecoin.

8.title: Decentralization's Last Stand
8.text: LUSD is one of the few stablecoins that can genuinely claim decentralization -- immutable contracts, ETH-only collateral, no governance keys, no admin functions. The trade-off is a modest market cap that makes it a rounding error in the stablecoin landscape. Liquity V2 launched BOLD as the successor with user-set interest rates and multi-collateral support. LUSD remains the philosophical benchmark against which every "decentralized" stablecoin should be measured, even as the market has clearly decided it prefers convenience over purity.

10.title: Scandal-Proof Somehow
10.text: Multiple hacks, a founder whose Wonderland treasury manager turned out to be a convicted fraudster from the QuadrigaCX collapse, and a governance token down 99% from its all-time high -- yet MIM still trades near peg. Abracadabra's model of lending against yield-bearing collateral remains clever in theory, but the protocol's security record reads like a cautionary tale for smart contract auditors. At this point, holding MIM requires less trust in the math and more faith in Daniele Sestagalli's ability to keep rebuilding after each crisis.

11.title: The Quiet Regulator's Pet
11.text: Paxos's original stablecoin is the definition of doing everything right and getting ignored for it. NYDFS-regulated since 2018, KPMG-audited, reserves in bankruptcy-remote accounts, monthly attestations -- and a market cap that barely moves the needle. Paxos's real business is issuing stablecoins for others (PayPal's PYUSD, formerly Binance's BUSD). USDP is less a product and more a proof of concept that Paxos can be trusted with your brand.

14.title: Justin Sun's Undying Dollar
14.text: USDD 2.0 emerged from its rocky algorithmic era with crypto collateral and a fresh governance model, though the centralized-dependent tag tells you Justin Sun still has the keys. It persistently trades above peg, which sounds good until you realize the premium reflects illiquidity as much as demand. The TRON ecosystem keeps it alive; whether that's a feature or a risk depends on your priors about its founder.

15.title: The Comeback CDP
15.text: Inverse Finance lost $24M across two oracle manipulation exploits in 2022, accumulating bad debt that would have buried most protocols. Instead, the DAO spent years clawing its way back -- selling tokens to investors, building the FiRM fixed-rate lending protocol, and launching a PSM backed by Sky's sUSDS. The sDOLA yield-bearing wrapper earning organic lending revenue is the kind of unsexy, sustainable DeFi that rarely makes headlines but actually works.

19.title: The Ghost Dollar
19.text: Gemini Dollar was one of the first NYDFS-regulated stablecoins, launched in 2018 with the Winklevoss seal of approval and State Street Bank custody. Years later it has a minimal market cap, near-zero DeFi presence, and exchange delistings that keep shrinking its already thin liquidity. Without aggressive exchange partnerships, GUSD is a museum piece: historically significant, technically sound, and gathering dust.

20.title: Time Pays Your Debt
20.text: Alchemix's self-repaying loans remain one of DeFi's most elegant ideas: deposit stablecoins, borrow up to 50%, and let yield gradually erase your debt. No liquidations, no interest payments -- just the slow passage of time converting future yield into present liquidity. The V3 upgrade nearly doubled capital efficiency, but the governance token trades at a fraction of its peak. alUSD is a stablecoin for patient DeFi users who've read the docs, which may explain why the broader market hasn't noticed.

22.title: The Longest Depeg
22.text: Synthetix's sUSD spent much of 2025 below peg after SIP-420 slashed the collateralization ratio from 750% to 200% and forgave staker debt. The structural incentive for stakers to buy discounted sUSD to repay their own debt -- the reflexive mechanism that maintained the peg for years -- was simply removed. Recovery plans involving exchange-fee buybacks and basis-trade vaults may work, but sUSD is now a case study in how upgrading peg mechanics mid-flight can go sideways.

23.title: The Passive Yield Play
23.text: Origin Dollar is the stablecoin that pays you to hold it -- no staking, no locking, just a rebasing balance that grows as the protocol deploys USDC into Morpho and Curve strategies. The clever twist is that smart contracts must explicitly opt in to receive yield, so OUSD held in non-opted AMM pools effectively subsidizes everyone else's returns. It's a well-engineered product for the small cohort of users who want DeFi yield without the DeFi homework.

24.title: The Mobile-First Dollar
24.text: Celo Dollar is what happens when you build a stablecoin around phone numbers instead of wallet addresses. The Mento reserve backing it holds USDC, DAI, BTC, ETH, and CELO at a reported 393% overcollateralization ratio -- impressive until you remember that a crypto-heavy reserve can evaporate fast in a downturn. Celo's migration to an Ethereum L2 gives cUSD access to a broader ecosystem, and validators like Google Cloud and Deutsche Telekom lend institutional credibility. With its current market cap, cUSD remains a niche stablecoin for emerging-market payments rather than a DeFi building block.

50.title: The Euro's Best On-Chain Bet
50.text: Circle's euro stablecoin brings the same reserve transparency and regulatory posture as USDC to the eurozone. MiCA-compliant and fully backed, EURC is positioning itself as the default EUR stablecoin before regulations force weaker competitors out. The euro stablecoin market is nascent enough that first-mover advantage still matters — and Circle is determined to be the name that sticks.

51.title: MiCA's Biggest Winner
51.text: Stasis Euro went from afterthought to contender largely because MiCA regulation cleared the field and EURS was already compliant. Malta-based, BDO-audited, and holding an EMI license since 2022, EURS was positioned for exactly this regulatory moment. The irony is that its explosive growth happened not because the product changed, but because competitors got disqualified. The looming threat is a consortium of European banks planning their own MiCA-compliant euro stablecoin, which would bring the kind of distribution that Stasis cannot match.

52.title: The Other Mento Euro
52.text: Celo Euro shares the same Mento reserve and algorithmic stability mechanism as cUSD, just pegged to the euro instead. With a small market cap and trading volumes that barely register outside of Celo-native DEXs, cEUR exists primarily to serve Celo's vision of region-specific stablecoins for mobile payments. The 393% overcollateralization ratio provides a generous buffer, but the crypto-heavy reserve composition means cEUR's stability in a severe downturn remains untested at any meaningful scale.

55.title: Angle's DeFi Euro
55.text: Angle Protocol's EURA is one of the few crypto-backed euro stablecoins — an overcollateralized design in a market dominated by RWA-backed issuers. Its centralized-dependent governance means community involvement with practical guardrails. For DeFi purists who want a euro without bank dependencies, EURA is one of the few options on the menu.

66.title: Frax's Inflation Hedge
66.text: Frax Price Index is pegged not to a currency but to the CPI — a stablecoin that tries to preserve purchasing power rather than nominal value. It's algorithmic, experimental, and philosophically interesting: why peg to a dollar that loses value annually when you can peg to the cost of living? The execution challenges of maintaining a CPI peg are considerable, but the concept alone makes FPI the most intellectually honest "stable" coin in the market.

75.title: Tezos's Quiet Giant
75.text: Youves' uUSD commands a dominant share of Tezos DeFi TVL, making it the largest protocol on a chain most people have forgotten about. The 300% overcollateralization in XTZ provides a generous safety margin. The catch is near-zero trading volume on major aggregators, reflecting the reality that uUSD is deeply liquid within its own ecosystem and essentially invisible outside it. It's a functioning, well-designed CDP stablecoin stranded on an island that the broader crypto market stopped visiting.

79.title: BNB Chain's CDP Bet
79.text: Lista DAO's lisUSD borrows MakerDAO's CDP playbook and transplants it to BNB Chain, where Binance's gravitational pull does the marketing. Collateral includes BNB, ETH, and liquid staking tokens, with a PSM accepting USDT, USDC, and FDUSD for peg stability. The plan to transition from MakerDAO's codebase to Liquity's is ambitious, and whether lisUSD can grow beyond Binance-subsidized adoption remains the central question.

98.title: Paxos's EU Passport
98.text: EUROe started as a Finnish EMI-regulated euro stablecoin from Membrane Finance, KPMG-audited and quietly competent. Then Paxos acquired Membrane Finance specifically to gain MiCA compliance across 30 European countries -- making EUROe less a standalone product and more Paxos's entry ticket to the EU market. Its future depends entirely on whether Paxos decides to scale EUROe as-is or rebrand it into its broader institutional stablecoin platform alongside USDP, PYUSD, and USDG.

101.title: Monerium's Electronic Money
101.text: Monerium's EURe is one of the few stablecoins licensed as electronic money in the EEA, meaning it's legally equivalent to a bank balance. It connects directly to IBAN accounts, making fiat on/off-ramps seamless in a way most stablecoins only promise. Its small scale belies its regulatory significance: EURe is what euro stablecoins look like when they actually comply with European financial law.

106.title: The Yield Mirage
106.text: Lybra Finance promised high APY just for holding eUSD, funded by ETH liquid staking yields flowing through to stablecoin holders. The protocol peaked at $400M TVL in 2023, then collapsed as yields compressed and attention moved elsewhere. eUSD now trades below peg with near-zero social activity, and the protocol offers USDC redemptions for eUSD holders -- the clearest possible signal of a wind-down. A cautionary tale about building a stablecoin around a yield narrative that couldn't survive a single market cycle.

110.title: Curve's Own Medicine
110.text: When the protocol that handles more stablecoin volume than anyone else launches its own stablecoin, the design better be interesting -- and crvUSD delivers. The LLAMMA mechanism replaces hard liquidations with gradual, continuous rebalancing through price bands, letting collateral be automatically rebought if prices recover. PegKeepers using USDC, USDT, and USDP manage the peg algorithmically, while the savings vault (scrvUSD) creates a self-correcting feedback loop where depeg pressure increases yields, attracting buyers back. It's the most technically sophisticated CDP stablecoin operating today.

118.title: Aave's Dollar
118.text: GHO is what happens when the largest lending protocol decides to mint its own stablecoin. Borrowers on Aave can mint GHO at favorable rates, creating a dollar tightly coupled to Aave's ecosystem health. The peg has been stable since the rocky first months, and stkAAVE discounts give governance participants a reason to borrow. It's DeFi-native in a way that few stablecoins genuinely are.

119.title: Binance's Current Favorite
119.text: First Digital USD rose to prominence as Binance's preferred stablecoin after BUSD's regulatory demise. Hong Kong-based and reserve-backed, it serves as the default trading pair on the world's largest exchange. Its fate is tied to Binance's continued endorsement — a single point of dependency that the market has apparently accepted.

120.title: Big Fintech's Entry Ticket
120.text: PayPal's stablecoin proves that when a payments giant with 400 million users issues a dollar token, people notice. Paxos-issued and fully reserved in treasuries and cash, PYUSD's regulatory credentials are impeccable. Its challenge isn't trust — it's utility. Until DeFi and PayPal's walled garden meaningfully converge, it risks being the best-credentialed stablecoin nobody uses on-chain.

122.title: The Yen's Only Option
122.text: GYEN is the world's first and essentially only regulated JPY-pegged stablecoin, issued by GMO Trust under a NYDFS trust charter with reserves at FDIC-insured banks. The market for a yen stablecoin is inherently niche -- Japan's own regulatory framework for stablecoins remains restrictive, and the JPY's persistent weakness against the dollar limits demand from non-Japanese users. GYEN's value proposition is less about competing with dollar stablecoins and more about being the only credible digital yen when someone finally needs one.

129.title: Ondo's Yield Machine
129.text: Ondo Finance's USDY offers tokenized US Treasury exposure to everyone outside the US, neatly sidestepping domestic securities law. It's RWA-backed, yield-bearing, and has become the poster child of the "tokenized treasuries" narrative. The irony of a product that democratizes US government debt by excluding US persons is apparently lost on no one.

145.title: Canada's Lonely Loonie
145.text: CADC is a 1:1 Canadian dollar stablecoin from PayTrie, backed by reserves at a tier-1 Canadian bank and registered with FINTRAC as a money services business. It's now on Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum, Base, and Solana. The Canadian stablecoin market is wide open -- the Bank of Canada has urged federal regulation -- and CADC's bet is that being the first compliant CAD stablecoin matters more than being the biggest.

146.title: The Basis Trade, Tokenized
146.text: Ethena's USDe pioneered the delta-neutral stablecoin: hold spot crypto, short the perps, pocket the funding rate. It works beautifully in bull markets when longs pay shorts handsomely for leverage. The catch? When funding flips negative — as it inevitably does — the insurance fund becomes the only thing between USDe and a death spiral. It's a sophisticated yield product wearing a stablecoin's clothing.

147.title: The Swiss Euro
147.text: Anchored Coins' AEUR offers a Swiss-regulated, reserve-backed euro stablecoin that targets the intersection of European money and Swiss financial infrastructure. Its smaller market cap belies a clean regulatory setup. In the euro stablecoin race, AEUR competes on jurisdiction prestige rather than distribution scale.

154.title: Sui's CDP Experiment
154.text: Bucket Protocol brings the MakerDAO playbook to the Sui ecosystem: deposit SUI, BTC, ETH, or LSTs, mint a dollar stablecoin at zero interest, get liquidated at 110% collateral ratio. The PSM module accepts USDC and USDT for peg stability, which is a polite way of saying the decentralized stablecoin ultimately leans on centralized ones when it matters. It's a competent CDP implementation searching for scale on a chain still searching for DeFi depth.

157.title: The Swiss Franc, Tokenized
157.text: VNX's VCHF is one of the first licensed Swiss franc stablecoins, issued out of Liechtenstein under FMA licenses. At modest market cap and daily volume measured in tens of thousands, VCHF is less a liquid trading instrument and more a proof-of-concept that CHF can exist on-chain. For the small audience that specifically needs a regulated Swiss franc token, it's one of the only games in town.

158.title: Liechtenstein's Quiet Euro
158.text: VNX Euro shares its sibling VCHF's regulatory pedigree under Liechtenstein's FMA. At thin liquidity, VEUR is dwarfed by Circle's EURC and the MiCA-compliant competition. Its multi-chain availability across Ethereum, Polygon, Avalanche, and Solana is a nice touch for a token that very few people are currently moving.

165.title: Australia's Dollar On-Chain
165.text: AUDD is one of those rare stablecoins that actually makes geographic sense: an Australian dollar token from an ASX-listed parent company (Novatti), audited by William Buck, and regulated under ASIC/AFSL. More interesting is its selection for the Reserve Bank of Australia's Project Acacia, testing tokenized asset settlement. Whether Australia's stablecoin market can sustain a domestic alternative to USD-denominated tokens is the macro question AUDD is quietly answering.

166.title: Base's Treasury Wrapper
166.text: Cygnus Finance's cgUSD is a yield-bearing stablecoin on Base backed by short-term US Treasury Bills, rebasing daily to reflect net asset value. It's the familiar RWA-stablecoin formula -- deposit USDC, get T-bill exposure -- dressed up with Chainlink price feeds and a subsidiary structure under ARKS Labs Foundation. The real test is whether Base users want yet another treasury-yield wrapper when the chain already hosts the issuer of the underlying USDC.

168.title: Volatility, Redistributed
168.text: f(x) Protocol's fxUSD takes a genuinely novel approach: split crypto collateral into a stable component (fxUSD) and a leveraged component (xPOSITION), shifting all volatility to the degens who want it. The V2 upgrade introduced up to 10x leverage positions, a delta-neutral Stability Pool, and fxSAVE for passive yield. The catch is that fxUSD's stability is only as good as the supply of leverage-hungry counterparties willing to absorb the volatility -- a dependency that works until it doesn't.

172.title: Blast's Yield Mirage
172.text: USDB was Blast L2's headline feature: bridge your stablecoins, get an auto-rebasing dollar token earning yield from MakerDAO's T-bill protocol. In theory, a stablecoin that grows while you hold it. In practice, Blast's TVL collapsed from its peak, and USDB's circulating supply shrank dramatically. The yield mechanics work as advertised; the problem is that the chain built around them failed to retain users after the airdrop farming ended. USDB is now a technically sound product on a chain the market has largely moved on from.

173.title: When BlackRock Calls It a Token
173.text: BlackRock's tokenized money market fund is what happens when the world's largest asset manager decides blockchain isn't a meme. BUIDL doesn't try to be a DeFi building block — it's institutional plumbing with an ERC-20 wrapper. When Larry Fink's firm validates tokenization, the rest of TradFi starts returning phone calls.

183.title: Bitcoin's CDP Outpost
183.text: BtcUSD is a Bitcoin-collateralized stablecoin that leverages cross-chain capabilities to exist across multiple EVM networks. Users deposit WBTC or BTCB into overcollateralized vaults to mint dollars -- a familiar CDP model applied specifically to Bitcoin holders who want liquidity without selling. At its current modest scale, the question is whether BTC holders will trust yet another wrapping layer when established CDPs like MakerDAO already accept wrapped Bitcoin.

185.title: The All-Weather Dollar
185.text: Gyroscope's GYD is an exercise in paranoid stablecoin design: a diversified reserve of sDAI, USDC, LUSD, and crvUSD, a primary-market AMM that algorithmically adjusts redemption prices during crises, and secondary-market AMMs that concentrate liquidity near the peg. The PAMM's circuit-breaker mechanism -- which reduces redemption rates during bank-run scenarios to preserve solvency -- is elegant game theory. GYD's thesis is that stablecoin design should optimize for surviving tail risks, not maximizing yield.

186.title: The Anti-Dollar Experiment
186.text: ISC deliberately rejects the USD peg in favor of tracking purchasing power through a basket of gold, bonds, T-bills, equities, and cash. The result is a flatcoin that appreciates over time rather than losing value to inflation -- a concept Brian Armstrong has championed but few have actually shipped. At minimal market cap on Solana, ISC is about as niche as stablecoins get. The variable peg and NAV-based pricing make it harder to use as a medium of exchange than a conventional dollar token.

195.title: The Usual Suspect
195.text: Usual's USD0 burst onto the scene promising a stablecoin where revenue flows back to tokenholders via the USUAL governance token. The RWA-backed reserves provide the peg stability, while the protocol's token economics provide the sizzle. It's an interesting governance experiment, though the December 2024 USD0++ depeg reminded everyone that innovative doesn't mean risk-free.

197.title: Resolving the Yield Question
197.text: Resolv's USR takes the delta-neutral approach with crypto backing, offering an alternative to Ethena's USDe for users who want basis-trade yields with a different risk profile. Its insurance pool and risk management framework attempt to address the perennial "what happens when funding goes negative" problem. In the basis-trade stablecoin niche, USR competes on risk structure rather than brand recognition.

202.title: Private Credit Meets DeFi
202.text: Anzen's USDz is backed by a private credit portfolio rather than the usual T-bills and cash, tapping into a market that crypto has barely touched. The yield is real, but so is the illiquidity risk inherent in private credit assets. The question every private-credit-backed stablecoin must answer: what happens during a credit crunch when those underlying loans stop performing?

205.title: The VanEck-Managed Dollar
205.text: Agora's AUSD has the resume that makes compliance departments swoon: VanEck manages the reserves, State Street provides custody, and Chaos Labs delivers real-time proof of reserves with on-chain attestations every 15 minutes. Its revenue-sharing model with distribution partners is the closest thing to a "Stablecoin 3.0" business model anyone has actually shipped. At growing circulation across multiple chains via LayerZero, AUSD is positioning itself as the institutional-grade alternative that doesn't sacrifice DeFi composability.

209.title: The Artist Formerly Known as DAI
209.text: Sky Dollar is MakerDAO's rebranded stablecoin, the culmination of Rune Christensen's "Endgame" vision to make the protocol more normie-friendly. Under the hood it's the same overcollateralized vaults and PSM modules — just with a fresh coat of paint and a governance structure that's still figuring itself out. Whether the rebrand was genius marketing or unnecessary complexity remains the market's most polite disagreement.

213.title: The Middleman's Stablecoin
213.text: M0's M token is a middleware play: rather than competing with USDC or USDT directly, it provides infrastructure for other stablecoins and fintechs to build on. Its RWA-backed reserves and centralized-dependent governance aim for a middle ground between Tether's opacity and Circle's centralization. The "protocol for stablecoins" pitch is elegant in theory — the question is whether the market wants a meta-stablecoin layer.

215.title: Cardano's Dollar Anchor
215.text: Moneta's USDM is the premier fiat-backed stablecoin on Cardano, co-issued by Norwegian Block Exchange under an EU e-money license for MiCA compliance. The Charli3 oracle verifying 1:1 reserves before each mint is a thoughtful on-chain guardrail that most stablecoins skip. It's a well-structured product constrained by Cardano's DeFi ecosystem size -- proving once again that the hardest part of launching a stablecoin isn't the backing, it's finding users.

218.title: The Purist's CDP
218.text: River's satUSD makes a deliberate choice: no centralized stablecoin collateral accepted, only BTC, ETH, BNB, and LSTs. Its Omni-CDP lets you deposit collateral on one chain and mint on another via LayerZero, eliminating bridge risk. The bull case writes itself -- a pure crypto-collateral CDP with cross-chain reach. The bear case is whether concentrated ecosystem dependencies and the absence of stablecoin collateral create fragility during sharp downturns.

219.title: Binance's Shadow Dollar
219.text: USDF, now under the Aster DEX rebrand, is a yield-bearing stablecoin whose USDT backing is deployed exclusively in delta-neutral strategies on Binance. The yields are attractive, but so is the concentration risk: every dollar of backing runs through Binance infrastructure with Ceffu holding the keys. It's a potent yield machine with a single, very large point of failure.

220.title: Bitcoin Banking, On-Chain
220.text: Avalon's USDa has quietly become one of the largest CDP projects by TVL, backed by BTC and Bitcoin LSTs with institutional credit lines from Asian conglomerates. The fixed 8% borrowing rate and 1:1 USDT redemption guarantee via institutional liquidity make it structurally distinct from typical CDPs. The CEX-based HFT liquidation engine is clever but means your stablecoin's stability ultimately depends on centralized exchange infrastructure.

221.title: Ethena's Safe Side
221.text: If USDe is the exciting sibling, USDtb is the responsible one — backed by BlackRock's BUIDL fund rather than delta-neutral trades. Ethena built it for users who want the ecosystem without the basis-trade risk, creating a safety valve that also serves as USDe's backstop. It's the stablecoin equivalent of keeping a boring index fund alongside your options portfolio.

225.title: RWA Restaking's First Bet
225.text: Zoth's ZeUSD bills itself as the first RWA restaking layer -- a CDP stable token minted against tokenized treasuries, ETFs, and money market funds that can then be restaked across DeFi for additional yield. The dual-yield model (off-chain T-bill interest plus on-chain restaking rewards) targets higher returns than vanilla stablecoin staking. Whether "restaking your restaked treasury token" is financial innovation or unnecessary complexity depends on your tolerance for recursive yield engineering.

226.title: Swiss Stubbornness, Tokenized
226.text: Frankencoin is a genuinely decentralized Swiss franc stablecoin — no foundation, no team tokens, no VC backing. Its auction-based liquidation mechanism and minimalist governance are a throwback to crypto's original ethos. The Swiss franc peg serves a niche audience, but Frankencoin proves that small, well-designed protocols can survive without a marketing budget.

230.title: The Rotating Yield Engine
230.text: Noon's USN is a delta-neutral stablecoin that rotates between funding-rate arbitrage and T-bill strategies based on market conditions. The "intelligent allocation" pitch is a more honest framing than most competitors offer -- acknowledging that no single yield source works in all market regimes. Transparent proof of solvency and zero VC pre-allocation is either genuinely aligned or a clever marketing angle; time will tell.

231.title: Berachain's Basket Dollar
231.text: HONEY is Berachain's native stablecoin, minted by depositing USDC, USDT0, pyUSD, or USDe into per-collateral vaults governed by BGT holders. It's less a novel stablecoin design and more a liquidity unification layer -- aggregating the chain's imported dollars into a single token that serves as Berachain's unit of account. HONEY's fate is entirely coupled to Berachain's success: if the chain's Proof-of-Liquidity model attracts sustained TVL, HONEY thrives as the default dollar; if not, it's just another wrapper nobody asked for.

234.title: The Payments Play
234.text: WSPN's Worldwide USD aspires to be the stablecoin for actual commerce, targeting trade finance and cross-border settlements rather than DeFi degens. Its white-label infrastructure lets enterprises issue their own branded stablecoins, which is either a clever platform play or an admission that WUSD itself lacks distribution. The market cap remains modest despite partnerships spanning Philippines exchanges to Australian commodity exporters, suggesting the "stablecoin payment network" thesis is still more pitch deck than protocol.

235.title: Frax Grows Up
235.text: After years of algorithmic experimentation that made regulators nervous and degens rich, Frax Finance went full TradFi with frxUSD -- a fully-backed stablecoin whose reserves sit in BlackRock's BUIDL fund, tokenized by Securitize. The DAO voted unanimously for the pivot, which tells you everything about where crypto's risk appetite has shifted. Sam Kazemian's stated ambition of applying for a Federal Reserve Master Account is either visionary or delusional, but the BlackRock backing lends it more credibility than most stablecoin founders' dreams.

237.title: Treasury Yields On-Chain
237.text: Hashnote's USYC is a tokenized money market fund that passes T-bill yields directly to holders. It's RWA-backed, yield-bearing, and about as exciting as its underlying asset — which is precisely the point. In a world of exotic DeFi yields, sometimes the most radical product is just a savings account with an ERC-20 wrapper.

239.title: Malta's Euro Bet
239.text: StablR's EURR is one of the early MiCA-compliant euro stablecoins, licensed through Malta's MFSA and backed by Tether's strategic investment -- a move that lets Tether maintain European presence without doing the compliance work itself. Grant Thornton audits and The Network Firm proof-of-reserves add credibility layers, though the real question is whether a Tether-backed entity can win institutional trust in a market built on regulatory purity.

240.title: The Dollar Sibling
240.text: StablR's USDR rides the same Malta EMI license and MiCA compliance infrastructure as its euro sibling EURR, offering a dollar-denominated option for European users who want regulatory certainty. Reserves sit with European financial institutions in cash and short-term government bonds, audited by Grant Thornton. It is a competent, regulation-first product in a market that increasingly rewards exactly that -- though differentiating a compliant USD stablecoin in a field of dozens remains the core challenge.

241.title: Treasury Yield, Repackaged
241.text: OpenEden's USDO is a regulated yield-bearing stablecoin with a Bermuda BMA license and TBILL-token backing that gives it genuine substance. The rebasing mechanism distributes T-bill yield daily by increasing holder balances -- elegant for retail, awkward for DeFi protocols that don't handle rebasing tokens, hence the cUSDO wrapper. Crossing $100M TVL within months of launch suggests the market has an appetite for transparent, tokenized-treasury stablecoins that aren't just institutional playthings.

245.title: Cardano's Dollar, Finally
245.text: USDA has been the stablecoin Cardano needed but couldn't quite ship, delayed by regulatory headwinds and operational handoffs. It finally went live with BitGo custody and no mint/burn fees. For a blockchain ecosystem that has long been criticized for lacking stablecoin infrastructure, USDA is a necessary step -- though limited U.S. state availability at launch suggests the regulatory path is far from complete.

246.title: The Falcon Play
246.text: Falcon Finance's USDf enters the delta-neutral arena alongside Ethena, offering yield through basis-trade strategies with a centralized-dependent governance model. Its crypto-backed structure means the peg relies on market dynamics rather than reserve transparency. In the crowded yield-bearing stablecoin space, differentiation is a question of execution speed and risk management.

247.title: France's MiCA Pioneer
247.text: Schuman Financial's EUROP is what happens when you build a euro stablecoin with the Banque de France looking over your shoulder. ACPR-licensed, KPMG-audited, and reserves held at Societe Generale, it checks every institutional box that MiCA demands -- plus an extra 2% reserve buffer beyond the 1:1 requirement. With euro stablecoins representing barely a fraction of the global stablecoin float, even the best-credentialed entrant faces a market that simply hasn't arrived yet.

249.title: Latin America's Bridge
249.text: Brazilian Digital's BRZ gives Brazil's crypto traders a real-denominated on-ramp without the volatility of converting through USD pairs. RWA-backed and centrally managed, it serves a practical need in one of crypto's most active retail markets. Its success is less about innovation and more about understanding that sometimes the simplest product wins.

250.title: Ripple's Dollar Bet
250.text: After years of fighting the SEC over XRP, Ripple launched its own stablecoin with NYDFS approval — a plot twist even Ripple skeptics didn't see coming. RLUSD is built for Ripple's payments network, aiming to be the bridge asset that XRP never became for institutional transfers. Fully reserved and centrally managed, it's less a DeFi primitive and more a cross-border payments tool.

251.title: Hyperliquid's Lending Layer
251.text: Felix Protocol forked Liquity V2 and deployed it on Hyperliquid L1, creating a CDP-based stablecoin that lets traders mint feUSD against HYPE, WBTC, ETH, and LSTs to use as margin. Growth from zero to substantial deposits within months is impressive, though much of it is inseparable from Hyperliquid's own ecosystem momentum. The Liquity-derived architecture adds proven liquidation mechanics, but the addition of centralized admin controls -- mint caps, emergency pausing -- means this is very much a modified fork, not a philosophical successor.

252.title: Delta-Neutral via CeFi
252.text: StandX's DUSD takes the Ethena playbook -- spot long, perps short, pocket the spread -- and runs it through centralized custodians and its own perpetual futures DEX. The team's Binance Futures and Goldman Sachs pedigree explains the institutional architecture: off-chain collateral management with exchange-provided leverage and strict margin controls. Any delta-neutral stablecoin is ultimately a bet that funding rates remain favorable more often than not.

253.title: Bitcoin's Borrowing Layer
253.text: BIMA's USBD lets Bitcoin holders access liquidity without selling their bags, using wrapped BTC derivatives as collateral in overcollateralized vaults with a 160-225% minimum ratio. The Liquity-style TroveManager architecture is battle-tested, though applying it to BTC derivatives rather than ETH introduces additional bridge and wrapper risk. The fundamental tension remains: the people most likely to hold BTC are often the least likely to lever it.

254.title: SocGen's Blockchain Experiment
254.text: EUR CoinVertible is issued by SG-FORGE, the digital asset arm of French banking giant Société Générale. It's a fully regulated, MiCA-compliant euro stablecoin from a systemically important bank — which is either the future of tokenized money or a corporate innovation lab's pet project. Either way, when a bank with over a trillion euros in assets issues a stablecoin, the industry takes notes.

255.title: Bitcoin-Margined Stability
255.text: Aegis's YUSD markets itself as a bitcoin-backed stablecoin independent from fiat banking, which is a bold framing for what is essentially a delta-neutral strategy using BTC-margined perpetual contracts. The real-time proof-of-reserves through Accountable's verification network is genuinely differentiated -- you can watch the custodial vaults and open positions in real time, which is more than most competitors offer. Its survival depends on the same funding-rate dynamics that govern every delta-neutral stablecoin.

256.title: Curve's Recursive Dollar
256.text: Resupply's reUSD, built by the Convex and Yearn teams, is a stablecoin for crvUSD power users who want to leverage their lending positions further. Deposit crvUSD into Curve Lend, use the position as collateral, mint reUSD, sell it for more crvUSD, repeat. It pushed crvUSD to all-time-high supply -- a testament to recursive DeFi appetite. The composability that makes reUSD powerful is the same composability that makes it fragile.

257.title: The Original T-Bill Token
257.text: OpenEden's TBILL is a tokenized money market fund with institutional-grade ratings, managed by BNY Investments. Access is restricted to KYC'd professional investors, which limits retail appeal but is precisely the point. At competitive APY on short-dated treasuries, TBILL is less a stablecoin and more a regulated fund that happens to be an ERC-20 -- and for its target audience, that distinction matters.

258.title: The Ruble's Digital Shadow
258.text: A7A5 is a ruble-pegged stablecoin that appeared seemingly from nowhere to claim a massive market cap. Its centralized governance and RWA backing make it structurally conventional, but the geopolitical context makes it anything but. In a sanctions-heavy environment, a large ruble stablecoin raises more questions than its sparse documentation answers.

262.title: The Presidential Stablecoin
262.text: World Liberty Financial's USD1 is backed by the Trump family brand and entered the market with all the subtlety you'd expect. It launched with RWA backing and centralized governance, positioning itself somewhere between a political statement and a financial product. The reserves are real, but the regulatory questions write themselves.

263.title: Hong Kong's Quiet Dollar
263.text: Hex Trust's USDX is built by one of Asia's most established digital asset custodians, licensed under Hong Kong's TCSP regime with reserves in short-term Treasury Bills. Its primary home is the Flare blockchain and the newer Ozean chain, where it doubles as the native gas token -- an unusual dual role for a stablecoin. With 270+ institutional clients and offices across five countries, Hex Trust has the distribution network; whether USDX can translate custodial relationships into stablecoin adoption is the open question.

266.title: Plume's Wrapped Dollar
266.text: pUSD is a straightforward USDC wrapper on Plume Chain, held 1:1 in a BoringVault with zero minting or redemption fees. It exists to give Plume's RWAfi ecosystem a canonical stablecoin without building reserve infrastructure from scratch -- pragmatic if unambitious. The integration of World Liberty Financial's USD1 as an additional reserve asset adds political flavor to what is otherwise a utilitarian design.

269.title: Decentralization, Immutable
269.text: Liquity V2's BOLD is the stablecoin for people who mean it when they say decentralized. No governance, no upgrades, no RWA exposure -- just ETH and liquid staking tokens in overcollateralized vaults with user-set interest rates. The immutability is a feature and a constraint: any bug discovered post-deployment requires a full redeployment. The yield amplification mechanic, where stability pool depositors can earn more than borrowers pay, is clever game theory that sets BOLD apart from the lending-market stablecoin crowd.

271.title: Avalanche's Quiet Contender
271.text: Avant's avUSD is a USDC-backed stable-value token on Avalanche that pairs with savUSD, its yield-bearing counterpart running DeFi-native strategies including cash-and-carry trades. Growing to significant value within its first year with zero management fees suggests competent execution, even if the value proposition -- deposit USDC, get a wrapped version, optionally earn yield -- isn't going to set anyone's imagination on fire. In the Avalanche ecosystem, being the default stable-value token is a defensible position, if a modest one.

272.title: The SEC-Registered Yield Coin
272.text: YLDS stands alone as one of the few yield-bearing stablecoins registered with the SEC as a security. This means actual regulatory clarity rather than the "move fast and hope for the best" approach most competitors take. The trade-off is operational constraints and restricted availability, but for institutions requiring regulatory certainty, YLDS is the rare stablecoin that comes with a blessing from Washington.

275.title: The Dutch Compliance Standard
275.text: Quantoz's USDQ holds the distinction of being issued from the only MiCA-licensed stablecoin jurisdiction with a AAA credit rating, supervised by De Nederlandsche Bank itself. Backed by Tether, Kraken, and Fabric Ventures, it combines institutional credibility with the pragmatic observation that European crypto users need dollar-denominated stablecoins too. The Visa principal membership for stablecoin-linked debit cards is the kind of distribution play that turns compliance into competitive advantage.

282.title: The Interchain Dollar
282.text: Noble's USDN is built on M0's stablecoin extension engine, making it a white-labeled version of M0's treasury-backed M token designed specifically for the Cosmos ecosystem. The yield-distribution model passes T-bill returns to holders, validators, and supporting platforms, creating incentive alignment that most stablecoins ignore entirely. Noble has already facilitated billions in stablecoin transfers across Cosmos, so the distribution infrastructure is proven. Whether the IBC-native approach can compete beyond Cosmos is the strategic gamble.

286.title: The Paxos Sequel
286.text: Global Dollar is Paxos's second act after BUSD, built to avoid the regulatory friction that killed its Binance partnership. Singapore-regulated and reserve-backed, USDG targets the institutional corridor that doesn't want Tether's opacity or Circle's SVB memories. Whether the market needs another compliant stablecoin is a question USDG is determined to answer anyway.

296.title: Cap's Yield Play
296.text: Cap Protocol's cUSD offers an RWA-backed stablecoin with a centralized-dependent governance model that routes yield back to holders. It operates in the increasingly crowded space of yield-bearing stablecoins, competing on distribution and integration rather than novelty. The protocol's bet is that a well-executed yield product can carve out space between the giants.

309.title: AI Meets RWA
309.text: USD.AI blends the two hottest crypto narratives — artificial intelligence and real-world assets — into a single stablecoin product. Its centralized-dependent governance suggests human oversight where it counts, while the AI branding does the marketing work. Whether the "AI" label reflects genuine innovation or narrative arbitrage is left as an exercise for the reader.

325.title: Binance's Euro
325.text: Eurite is the euro stablecoin endorsed by Binance, giving it instant distribution to the world's largest exchange. Issued by Banking Circle and regulated in the EU, it's MiCA-ready from day one. Whether Binance's distribution muscle can make a euro stablecoin stick where others have struggled remains the open question.

336.title: The Aggregator Dollar
336.text: United Stables takes the yield-aggregation approach, pooling reserves across multiple strategies and passing the returns to holders. It's a bet that diversification of stablecoin backing is itself a feature worth tokenizing. Simple concept, hard execution.
